text: This is Kaava. Ask a construction drawing a question, and get a number that is computed, never generated.

How many windows are on this floor? Twelve, counted from the drawing's own geometry, and numbered on the plan and in the model raised from it. The answer is marked Verified. That is a measured claim: on drawings held back for testing, counts of this kind were wrong eight times in more than five thousand.
Areas work the same way. This corridor runs around a lift, so the lift is cut out of it: thirteen point nine nine square metres.
Stoa's own sheets are harder. This slab's area comes from its printed dimensions. Two examiners then look inside it and find two trenches. The program measures them on the drawing and takes them out.

Here the question gives a single size: one door, one point seven metres wide. The program measures that door in pixels, then the hall with it. Two hundred and forty-four square metres, within half a percent of what the sheet's own scale bar gives.

Every door of a school, boxed tile by tile. A count read from pixels can move from run to run, so it is marked Check this, never Verified. Every box is on the sheet, so a person can check each one, and leave out what does not belong.

On the same two hundred questions, a vision model alone is right sixty-two point five percent of the time. Kaava is right ninety-five point eight percent of the time, at forty percent of the cost. Of nearly seventeen thousand Verified answers on our development drawings, none was wrong.
Numbers computed, never generated. Evidence you can check in seconds. Kaava.
